text: Last time, a matrix became a motion of the plane, a record of where i hat and j hat land. A natural next question is what happens when you perform one motion and then another, say a quarter turn followed by a shear. The grid lines are still straight, parallel and evenly spaced at the end, so the combined motion must itself be a linear transformation, with a matrix of its own.

Let us watch it. First the rotation: i hat swings up to zero, one, and j hat swings left to minus one, zero. Then, starting from wherever things now sit, the shear pushes the plane sideways, sliding every point to the right by its height. Follow i hat through both steps, and it ends up at one, one. Follow j hat, and it ends up back at minus one, zero.

Those two landing spots are all we need, because they are the columns of the combined matrix, one, one, and minus one, zero. One matrix now does the work of two. We call this new matrix the product of the shear and the rotation, and the act of applying one transformation after another is called composition, much as two legs of a journey combine into a single route.

Notice how we write it. The rotation happens first, yet it sits on the right, next to the vector, and the shear sits on the left. That is because, as with functions, the matrix closest to the vector acts on it first. Reading a product from right to left, the way the vector experiences it, removes most of the confusion people have with matrix multiplication.

We can now compute the product without memorising anything. The first column of the product is where i hat ends up, so take the rotation's first column, which is where i hat went after the first step, and feed it through the shear. Then do the same with the second column. In other words, the left matrix acts on each column of the right matrix, one column at a time.

Watch it on the numbers. The rotation's first column is zero, one, so we take zero copies of the shear's first column plus one copy of its second, which gives one, one. The rotation's second column is minus one, zero, so we take minus one copy of the shear's first column, which gives minus one, zero. Each column of the answer is just the matrix times vector rule from the last lesson, applied again.

Now swap the order, and shear first, then rotate. Watch the grid. This time i hat ends up at zero, one, and j hat ends up at minus one, one, which is a different place, so the product is a different matrix. Order matters in matrix multiplication, just as putting on socks and then shoes is not the same as shoes and then socks. In symbols, A times B is usually not B times A.

What does not matter is how you group a longer chain. Applying three transformations in a row gives the same final motion whether you first combine the first pair or the last pair, because either way the vector goes through the same motions in the same order. This property is called associativity, and it lets us collapse any chain of matrices into a single one.

That fact explains a design choice in every neural network. Two layers that only multiply by matrices collapse into a single matrix, so stacking them buys nothing new. Real networks put a gentle bend, called a nonlinearity, between the layers, precisely so that the chain cannot be folded into one matrix, and depth gives genuinely new power. Inside a transformer, much of the work in every layer is matrix multiplication, separated by bends like these.

So multiplying matrices means doing one motion after another, with the right hand matrix acting first, and each column of the product is where a basis arrow finally lands. Next, we ask how much a transformation stretches or squashes area, which is measured by a single number called the determinant.
